name: IPEX syndrome
aliases: immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked syndrome

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard immunology references
clinicalPearls: IPEX syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by mutations in FOXP3, the master transcription factor for regulatory T cells
Loss of functional regulatory T cells leads to severe, early-onset systemic autoimmunity affecting multiple organs
The classic triad is severe enteropathy with intractable watery diarrhoea, early-onset endocrinopathy (especially neonatal type 1 diabetes and thyroiditis), and eczematous dermatitis
It typically presents in male infants and can be rapidly life-threatening from malabsorption, failure to thrive, and metabolic derangement
Additional autoimmune features include haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, nephropathy, and hepatitis
Infections may occur, partly reflecting the underlying immune dysregulation and partly the intensive immunosuppression used to control the disease
The autoimmune enteropathy often shows characteristic small-bowel histology with villous atrophy and does not respond to dietary exclusion alone
Treatment relies on immunosuppression (for example calcineurin inhibitors and sirolimus) to control disease, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering the only definitive cure
reference.pathophysiology: IPEX syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in FOXP3 on the X chromosome, the transcription factor essential for the development and function of CD4-positive CD25-positive regulatory T cells. Without functional regulatory T cells, peripheral tolerance collapses and autoreactive effector T cells drive widespread tissue-specific autoimmunity. The resulting immune attack on the gut epithelium, endocrine organs (pancreatic islets, thyroid), skin, blood cells, and kidneys produces the characteristic multi-organ autoimmune phenotype. Because the defect is one of immune regulation rather than a simple failure of host defence, the dominant problem is aggressive autoimmunity from early infancy, though secondary infection is common.
additionalDifferentials: Other monogenic autoimmune enteropathies and IPEX-like syndromes (for example CD25 or STAT deficiencies)
Severe combined immunodeficiency with enteropathy such as Omenn syndrome
Cow's milk protein enteropathy and other infantile enteropathies
Congenital infections causing failure to thrive
additionalInvestigations: FOXP3 genetic testing and analysis of FOXP3 protein expression
Enumeration and functional assessment of regulatory T cells
Autoantibody panels (including anti-enterocyte and endocrine autoantibodies)
Blood glucose, thyroid function, and other endocrine screening
Full blood count and haemolysis screen for autoimmune cytopenias
redFlags: Intractable diarrhoea with dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and failure to thrive as a neonatal emergency
Neonatal or early-onset diabetes with metabolic decompensation
Live vaccines should be avoided given the immune dysregulation and immunosuppressive therapy
reference.prognosis: Untreated IPEX is frequently fatal in infancy or early childhood from enteropathy, metabolic complications, and infection; immunosuppression can achieve temporary control, but haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally undertaken early, provides the best prospect of long-term survival.
pitfalls: Attributing intractable infantile diarrhoea to food allergy and missing autoimmune enteropathy
Overlooking a monogenic cause of neonatal diabetes in a boy with multi-organ autoimmunity
Delaying genetic testing and transplant referral in a critically ill infant
Confusing IPEX with APECED, which is autosomal recessive, AIRE-related, and presents later
management: Control the autoimmunity with immunosuppression using corticosteroids together with a calcineurin inhibitor or sirolimus as a bridge to definitive treatment
Pursue allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation early, as it offers the only prospect of cure
Manage the enteropathy with parenteral nutrition and fluid and electrolyte support for intractable diarrhoea and failure to thrive
Treat the endocrinopathy with insulin for neonatal diabetes and thyroid hormone replacement for autoimmune thyroiditis
Manage autoimmune cytopenias and provide intensive skin care for the eczematous dermatitis
Give infection prophylaxis and treat intercurrent infection promptly, reflecting both immune dysregulation and iatrogenic immunosuppression
Offer genetic counselling and FOXP3 testing, with maternal carrier and family testing for this X-linked disorder
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across immunology, gastroenterology, endocrinology and transplantation
